text: Agostina Pietrantoni (27 March 1864 – 13 November 1894), born Livia Pietrantoni, was an Italian religious sister of the Sisters of Divine Charity. She was born on 27 March 1864 in Pozzaglia Sabina, about 50 kilometres north-east of Rome, as the second of eleven children to Francesco Pietrantoni and Caterina Costantini. She received her First Communion in 1868 and Confirmation in 1876. Pietrantoni began working in 1871 doing manual labour for road construction and later, in 1876, travelled to Tivoli with other adolescent seasonal workers during the winter months for the olive harvest. She refused marriage offers, despite her mother's insistence, and in January 1886 travelled to Rome with her priest uncle Matteo to enter consecrated life. After sending a letter of admission to the Sisters of Divine Charity, her request was declined; however, she persisted and was eventually accepted into the congregation. She left for Rome again and joined the Sisters of Divine Charity in the Via Santa Maria in Cosmedin on 23 March 1886, assuming the religious name Agostina upon her clothing ceremony on 13 August 1887. She was assigned as a nurse to the Santo Spirito Hospital in Rome on 13 August 1887 and remained there until her death. While working in the tuberculosis ward, she contracted the disease and recovered, then was sent to the ward herself in 1889 to care for patients. On one occasion, she was attacked and beaten after seizing a knife from a patient, despite the other religious members' concerns. The male patient Giuseppe Romanelli began harassing her and sent her death threats. On the evening of 12 November 1894, the sisters asked her to take time off due to concern for her safety; she refused. Romanelli attacked and stabbed her to death in the morning of 13 November 1894, stabbing her three times in the shoulder and left arm, once in the jugular, and finally in the chest. Moments before her death, she forgave her killer. Professor Achille Ballori, who had previously warned her about Romanelli, examined her remains and noted that "Sister Agostina has allowed herself to be slaughtered like a lamb," observing no contractions of her nerves or heart. Her funeral blocked the streets of Rome, with thousands lining the route and kneeling before her casket; a report in the Messaggero newspaper on 16 November stated that "never a more impressive spectacle was seen in Rome." Her remains were moved to the generalate on 3 February 1941 and, following her canonisation, to her hometown on 14 November 2004. Agostina's spiritual writings were approved by theologians on 28 May 1941. The beatification process began on 14 December 1945 under Pope Pius XII, and Pope Paul VI declared her "venerable" on 19 September 1968 and presided over her beatification on 12 November 1972. A miracle attributed to her intercession was investigated and validated by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints on 19 March 1996, with assent from the medical board on 17 April 1997, a panel of theologians on 7 October 1997, and the Congregation on 20 January 1998. Pope John Paul II approved the miracle on 6 April 1998, and Agostina was canonised on 18 April 1999. St Agostina was declared the patron saint for nurses in Italy on 20 May 2003 following deliberations by the Italian Episcopal Conference.
